16        All defendants now move to dismiss Realtek’s complaint for failure to state a claim. See

18   claims pursuant to California Code of Civil Procedure § 425.16. Defendants also move the Court

23                              Legal Standard                             
24        A complaint that does not state a plausible claim upon which relief can be granted can be 
25   dismissed under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6). “A claim has facial plausibility when 
26   the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the 
27   defendant is liable.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). Legal conclusions “can provide 
1   Court must “accept all factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe the pleadings in the 
2   light most favorable to the nonmoving party.” Rowe v. Educ. Credit Mgmt. Corp., 559 F.3d 1028, 
3   1029–30 (9th Cir. 2009).                                              
4        “Generally, district courts may not consider material outside the pleadings when assessing 
5   the sufficiency of a complaint.” Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 998 (9th Cir. 
6   2018). But there are two exceptions.                                  
7        First, Federal Rule of Evidence 201 permits judicial notice of “a fact that is not subject to 
8   reasonable dispute” because the fact is “generally known” or “can be accurately and readily 
9   determined from sources whose accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned.” A court may take 
10   notice of “undisputed matters of public record,” but not of “disputed facts stated in public 
11   records.” Lee v. City of L.A., 250 F.3d 668, 690 (9th Cir. 2001) (emphasis in original). Thus, 
12   “when a court takes judicial notice of another court’s opinion, it may do so not for the truth of the 
13   facts recited therein, but for the existence of the opinion.” Id. (cleaned up).  
14        Second, the doctrine of incorporation by reference permits a court to treat an extrinsic 
15   document as if it were part of the complaint if the pleading “refers extensively to the document” or 
16   if “the document forms the basis” of a claim. Khoja, 899 F.3d at 1002. Incorporation can be proper 
17   “when assessing the sufficiency of a claim requires that the document at issue be reviewed,” but is 
18   not warranted when “the document merely creates a defense to the well-pled allegations.” Id. 
19   Incorporation by reference “is designed to prevent artful pleading by plaintiffs” but should not be 
20   used as a “tool for defendants to short-circuit the resolution of a well-pleaded claim.” Id. at 1003.

5   II.  Noerr-Pennington Immunity Bars Realtek’s Claims.                 
6        In moving to dismiss Realtek’s Sherman Act claims, defendants primarily argue that the 
7   conduct on which those claims are premised involved First Amendment-protected petitioning that 
8   cannot form a basis for federal antitrust claims or related state-law claims under the so-called 
9   “Noerr-Pennington” doctrine. See, e.g., United Mine Workers v. Pennington, 381 U.S. 657, 669–
10   70 (1965); Eastern R. R. Presidents Conf. v. Noerr Motor Freight Inc., 365 U.S. 127, 135–40 
11   (1961). The Court agrees.3                                            
12        The Noerr-Pennington doctrine “allows private citizens to exercise their First Amendment 
13   rights to petition the government without fear of antitrust liability.” Kaiser Found. Health Plan, 
14   Inc. v. Abbott Lab’ys, Inc., 552 F.3d 1033 (9th Cir. 2009). Under Noerr-Pennington, “those who 
15   petition any department of the government for redress are generally immune from statutory 
16   liability for their petitioning conduct.” Sosa v. DIRECTV, Inc., 437 F.3d 923, 929 (9th Cir. 2006). 
17   Courts must “construe federal statutes so as to avoid burdening the conduct that implicates the 
18   protections afforded by the Petition Clause unless the statute clearly provides otherwise.” Id. This 
19   immunity can extend to state law claims as well. Theme Promotions, Inc. v. News Am. Mktg. FSI, 
20   546 F.3d 991, 1007 (9th Cir. 2008) (“Noerr–Pennington doctrine applies to … state law tortious 
21   interference with prospective economic advantage claims.”).           
22        “In determining whether the burdened conduct falls under the protection of the Petition 
23   Clause,” courts must “give adequate ‘breathing space’ to the right to petition.” Sosa, 437 F.3d at 
24   931–32. The alleged conduct that forms the basis for Realtek’s claims here includes Future Link’s 
25

2   one million dollars upon the initiation of a lawsuit against Realtek or another of MediaTek’s 
3   competitors, and MediaTek’s alleged statements to a customer about that litigation. See Dkt. No. 
4   47-2, at 15–21 (MediaTek); Dkt. No. 57-10, 14–22 (Future Link).4 Because initiating and 
5   participating in litigation is one method of petitioning the government, litigation-related conduct 
6   falls within the scope of Noerr-Pennington.                           
7        Crucially, the protection afforded by Noerr-Pennington is not limited to active litigation. 
8   Instead, both the Supreme Court and the Ninth Circuit have “reject[ed] burdens on the right to 
9   petition the courts even where no actual litigation was pending.” Sosa, 437 F.3d at 937. In Liberty 
10   Lake Investments, Inc. v. Magnuson, 12 F.3d 155 (9th Cir. 1993), for example, the Ninth Circuit 
11   held that Noerr-Pennington immunity extended to a defendant who had funded anticompetitive 
12   litigation but was not a party to that litigation and therefore had not petitioned the courts directly. 
13   Similarly, in Sosa v. DIRECTV, the Ninth Circuit held that Noerr-Pennington immunity extends to 
14   “litigation-related activities preliminary to the formal filing of the litigation.” 437 F.3d at 937.

21   (1963)). Realtek’s argument, however, cannot be squared with the Ninth Circuit’s decision in 
22   Liberty Lake. In that case a third-party major shareholder of a company that owned shopping 
23   centers “prompted and paid for” “a last-minute appeal to the Spokane Board of County 
24   Commissioners” and “litigation in the Washington state courts alleging that the Liberty Lake

11   Sosa, 437 F.3d at 935. Realtek’s cited cases involving settlement agreements are inapposite, as 
12   they stand for the simple proposition that the mere fact that an agreement was reached to settle 
13   litigation will not immunize terms governing non-petitioning activity from antitrust scrutiny. 
14        Realtek separately contends that MediaTek’s disparaging communications with Realtek’s 
15   customers are not protected because they did not affect or advance Future Value’s litigation. Dkt. 
16   No. 64-2, at 14–15; Dkt. No. 66-2, 15–16 (citing Wisk Aero LLC v. Archer Aviation Inc., No. 
17   3:21-CV-02450_WHO, 2021 WL 4932734, at *7–9 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 14, 2021)). The Ninth Circuit 
18   has explained that “in the litigation context, not only petitions sent directly to the court in the 
19   course of litigation, but also ‘conduct incidental to the prosecution of the suit’ is protected by the 
20   Noerr-Pennington doctrine.” Sosa, 437 F.3d at 934. Accordingly, “communications between 
21   private parties are sufficiently within the protection of the Petition Clause to trigger the Noerr–
22   Pennington doctrine, so long as they are sufficiently related to petitioning activity.” Id. at 935.  
23        By Realtek’s own allegations, the purportedly anticompetitive communications between 
24   MediaTek and third parties all involved the ongoing patent litigation between Realtek and Future 
25   Link. The communications were thus “related” to that petitioning activity and are protected by 
26   Noerr-Pennington to the extent that they contributed to Future Link’s litigation efforts.5 But given 
27                                                                         
1   that MediaTek was not a party to that litigation, it is unclear how its communications could have 
2   contributed to the litigation. Even if MediaTek’s communications with third parties were too 
3   peripheral to the Future Link litigation to justify application of Noerr-Pennington, however, 
4   Realtek’s sparse allegations—which do not identify any of the specific third parties with whom 
5   MediaTek communicated or the specific contents of those communications—fail to state a 
6   plausible claim for relief or provide defendants with notice sufficient to permit their preparation of

8        That conduct falls within the scope of Noerr-Pennington does not necessarily preclude 
9   Realtek’s claims. “Neither the Petition Clause nor the Noerr-Pennington doctrine protects sham 
10   petitions, and statutes need not be construed to permit them.” Sosa, 437 F.3d at 932; This “‘sham’ 
11   exception to Noerr encompasses situations in which persons use the governmental process—as 
12   opposed to the outcome of that process—as an anticompetitive weapon.” City of Columbia v. 
13   Omni Outdoor Advert., Inc., 499 U.S. 365, 380 (1991) (emphasis in original).

8        Realtek argues that the sham series exception applies to its claim because Future Link filed 
9   “multiple lawsuits for an improper purpose regardless of merit.” Dkt. No. 64-2, 15–18; Dkt. No. 
10   66-2, at 16–18 (citing USS-POSCO).6 There are three problems with Realtek’s argument. 
11        First, Realtek’s allegation that the defendants conspired to monopolize the market for TV 
12   semiprocessors is premised on the litigation incentive in their license agreement. By the 
13   agreement’s own terms, however, MediaTek owed Future Link the full amount of the incentive 
14   upon the filing of a single initial lawsuit against Realtek. The litigation incentive therefore did not 
15   provide Future Link or IPValue with any reason to pursue a series of additional lawsuits against 
16   Realtek, and Realtek has not alleged other facts plausibly explaining why or how MediaTek 
17   caused Realtek to initiate the subsequent lawsuits.                   
18        Second, it is doubtful that the number of actions here is sufficient to constitute a “series” 
19   for purposes of the sham exception. The Complaint alleges that Future Link filed two patent 
20   infringement suits against Realtek in the Western District of Texas and a related action before the 
21   International Trade Commission (ITC), and that Future Link filed an infringement action in Japan 
22   through a subsidiary, Monterey Research LLC. Compl. ¶¶ 26, 31, 40. The Ninth Circuit has held 
23   that “[t]wo sham suits cannot amount to ‘a whole series of legal proceedings’ or a ‘pattern of 
24   baseless, repetitive claims.’” Int’l Longshore & Warehouse Union v. ICTSI Or., Inc., 863 F.3d 
25   1178, 1187 (9th Cir. 2017); cf. USS-POSCO, 31 F.3d at 811 (suggesting that sham series

4        The purpose of the series exception is to protect parties from the “crushing burden” that a

14        Third, the sham exception “encompasses situations in which persons use the governmental 
15   process—as opposed to the outcome of that process—as an anticompetitive weapon.” Omni 
16   Outdoor Advert., 499 U.S. at 380 (emphasis in original); see also USS-POSCO, 31 F.3d at 811 
17   (when considering “series” version of the sham exception to Noerr-Pennington, courts ask if “the 
18   legal filings [were] made, not out of a genuine interest in redressing grievances, but as part of a 
19   pattern or practice of successive filings undertaken essentially for purposes of harassment”). 
20   Realtek’s allegations suggest, however, that the defendants genuinely desired the relief sought in 
21   the four proceedings. See, e.g., Compl. ¶ 65 (“To MediaTek’s benefit, Future Link sought 
22   injunctions and an exclusion order limiting Realtek’s ability to make and sell Chips that 
23   incorporated the allegedly infringing technologies, including its TV Chips, and prohibiting 
24   outright Realtek’s end users from importing into the United States devices that include the accused 
25   technologies within Realtek’s TV Chips.”). To evade Noerr-Pennington, Realtek must identify the 
26   specific ways in which the defendants used the litigation itself—rather than the relief sought

2        For these reasons, the “sham series” exception to Noerr-Pennington does not apply to the 
3   defendants’ litigation-related conduct, and Noerr-Pennington bars each of the claims asserted in 
4   Realtek’s Complaint. See Theme Promotions, 546 F.3d at 1007 (“[B]ecause Noerr–Pennington 
5   protects federal constitutional rights, it applies in all contexts, even where a state law doctrine 
6   advances a similar goal.”).8 The Court therefore grants defendants’ motions to dismiss with leave 
7   to amend.
